## Original idea
{
  "title": "Domain-Adaptive Autoformalization via Subdomain-Conditioned Retrieval and Error Taxonomy",
  "core_problem": "Current autoformalization systems treat all mathematical subdomains identically, yet empirical evidence from MSC-180 (CV values 4–6× above high-variability thresholds across 60 mathematical branches) and FormalMATH (0% on discrete math vs. 50% on algebra for Goedel-Prover) reveals severe, systematic domain bias. Aria (ICLR 2026) independently confirms this: 42.9% on homological conjectures while all baselines (Gemini-2.5-Pro, Goedel-Formalizer-V2-32B, Kimina-Autoformalizer-7B) achieve 0% — demonstrating that certain specialized domains are catastrophically underserved even by SOTA systems. Shebzukhov (2026; arXiv 2603.24372) provides complementary evidence via cycle consistency fine-tuning on FineLeanCorpus: number theory achieves 0.722 cycle consistency vs. calculus at 0.516, confirming domain-dependent performance variation — but this observational analysis reports only aggregate performance per domain without analyzing how error types differ across subdomains. IndiMathBench (Biyani et al., 2025; arXiv 2512.00997) provides further corroboration: static category-specific Mathlib context boosts syntactic compilation rates dramatically (e.g., Claude Opus 4: 4.1% → 77.9%) but BEq semantic correctness is only 17.3% (54/312 problems) and deeply domain-biased — only 12 of 98 geometry problems achieve BEq success among top models vs. far higher rates for algebra and number theory — demonstrating that even rudimentary domain awareness improves compilation but the harder semantic correctness gap persists with clear domain structure. Meanwhile, retrieval-augmented approaches address retrieval quality through increasingly sophisticated methods — CRAMF uses contextual query augmentation for concept-level disambiguation, DRIFT (ICLR 2026) decomposes statements into ~5.8 atomic sub-queries for targeted concept-level retrieval, LeanSearch v2 (May 2026) achieves SOTA premise retrieval (nDCG@10 = 0.623) without any domain-specific fine-tuning via hierarchy-informed informalization, and LeanPremise/LeanHammer (ICLR 2026; arXiv 2506.07477) achieves 79.4% relative proof rate on OOD benchmarks via neural premise selection for Lean proving — but none conditions retrieval ranking on the inferred mathematical subdomain of the input problem in a dynamic, per-problem fashion for autoformalization. The 260k repair tuples in APRIL contain an explicit 'error_type' field encoding mutation categories (lme: line mutation errors, mlme: multi-line mutation errors, thme: theorem substitution errors, tme: tactic mutation errors) and an 'error' field with raw Lean compiler messages (e.g., 'type mismatch', 'unknown constant', 'tactic rewrite failed', 'unsolved goals'), but these have never been cross-tabulated by mathematical subdomain despite the dataset containing explicit Mathlib module paths in each tuple's 'path' field. Can we build the first autoformalization pipeline that systematically conditions its dynamic retrieval ranking and prompting signals on inferred mathematical subdomain — beyond both static category context (IndiMathBench) and concept-level disambiguation/decomposition (CRAMF/DRIFT) — and can we provide the first domain-stratified cross-tabulation of APRIL's existing error categories plus a finer-grained error taxonomy extracted from raw Lean compiler messages, characterizing how autoformalization error TYPES distribute across mathematical subdomains with statistical rigor, going beyond observational domain-stratified scores (Shebzukhov, 2026)?",
  "opportunity": "Six critical resources and findings converged in 2025–2026 that make domain-adaptive autoformalization both feasible and necessary, each containing underexploited domain metadata: (1) Herald (ICLR 2025) provides 580k NL-formal pairs where Mathlib4 module paths can be recovered by parsing qualified theorem names from formal statements (e.g., extracting 'Topology.Basic' from theorem names like 'Topology.Basic.isOpen_compl') — the released HuggingFace dataset (FrenzyMath/Herald_statements) contains id, informal_statement, and formal_statement fields without an explicit module path column, requiring parsing or re-running the Lean-Jixia extraction pipeline; (2) FineLeanCorpus/CriticLean (2025) provides 286k verified entries (509k total) with hierarchical problem-level domain labels and difficulty scores — but these capture mathematical topic, not formalization-level structure; (3) APRIL (Feb 2026) provides 260k repair tuples (59.5% theorem substitution errors, plus tactic, multi-line, and line mutations) with an explicit 'path' field encoding Mathlib module paths per tuple AND an existing 'error_type' field classifying mutation categories (lme/mlme/thme/tme) plus a raw 'error' field containing Lean compiler messages — making it the most immediately usable source for domain-stratified error analysis, as module paths can be directly mapped to mathematical subdomains without additional parsing, and our taxonomy contribution builds on APRIL's existing error categorization by cross-tabulating these mutation categories with mathematical subdomain and constructing a finer-grained taxonomy from the raw compiler error messages (parsing semantic categories such as typeclass resolution failures, coercion mismatches, tactic incompatibilities from raw strings like 'type mismatch', 'unknown constant', 'unsolved goals'); (4) CRAMF's 26k-definition knowledge base stores module paths (θ_p) per definition and uses LLM-generated contextual query augmentation to disambiguate polysemous concepts, but never conditions its retrieval reranking (bge-reranker-v2-m3) on the mathematical subdomain of the input problem; (5) MathAtlas (May 2026) provides 52k entities across 87 math areas with 178k dependency relations, using domain labels only for evaluation not pipeline conditioning; (6) LeanSearch v2 (May 2026) achieves SOTA domain-agnostic premise retrieval via hierarchy-informed Mathlib informalization — but its success demonstrates that retrieval quality alone does not address the domain bias problem documented by MSC-180 and FormalMATH, because domain bias manifests in formalization accuracy, not retrieval recall; and (7) IndiMathBench (Biyani et al., 2025; arXiv 2512.00997) demonstrates that static category-specific Mathlib context dramatically improves compilation rates for 4 mathematical domains — proving domain awareness helps — but uses one-time static context blocks with human-labeled categories rather than dynamic per-problem conditioning, and its BEq results (17.3% for Claude Opus 4, 54/312) reveal a persistent syntactic-vs-semantic gap with strong domain bias (geometry: 12/98 BEq among top models), leaving the semantic correctness challenge unaddressed. Note: IndiMathBench is an arXiv preprint (desk-rejected from ICLR 2026); its compilation and domain-bias patterns are corroborated by peer-reviewed evidence from MSC-180, FormalMATH, and Aria. Crucially, MSC-180 (Dec 2025) quantified domain bias with coefficient of variation metrics across 60 mathematical branches showing best models achieve only 18.89% overall with maximum 41.7% domain coverage, FormalMATH (2025) showed Goedel-Prover achieving 50% on algebra but 0% on discrete math, and Aria's homological conjectures results (42.9% vs. 0% for all baselines) provide the strongest peer-reviewed evidence that domain-specialized problems require fundamentally different handling. Shebzukhov (2026; arXiv 2603.24372) corroborates domain performance variation via cycle consistency fine-tuning — number theory at 0.722 vs. calculus at 0.516 — but performs only post-hoc observational analysis with no domain conditioning or error type classification. LeanPremise/LeanHammer (ICLR 2026; arXiv 2506.07477) provides further evidence of domain-dependent difficulty in the Lean ecosystem: its neural premise selection achieves strong average OOD performance (20.7% on miniCTX-v2) but with dramatic project-level variation (Carleson 0%, Foundation 38%, ConNF 16%, FLT 36.4%), confirming that domain-specific challenges persist even for state-of-the-art retrieval/selection systems — though LeanHammer targets proving (premise selection for tactic-based proof search) rather than autoformalization. KELPS (ICML 2025 AI4Math Workshop; arXiv 2507.08665) achieves 88.9% syntactic accuracy (pass@1) on MiniF2F via Knowledge Equations as intermediate representation, outperforming DeepSeek-V3 (81%) and Herald (81.3%) — but is entirely domain-agnostic with no subdomain conditioning, operating across 6 math topics without analyzing domain-specific error patterns. The ICML 2026 AI4Math Workshop validates growing community interest in domain-aware autoformalization evaluation through two complementary challenge tracks: Track 4 (ShadowBench) evaluates end-to-end autoformalization across 8 mathematical areas with semantic alignment pass rate metrics; Track 1 (FormalRx) evaluates semantic alignment preservation using the FormalRx-Test dataset built on a 28-category SCI Error Taxonomy that classifies errors by type. ConNF (DDR, ICLR 2025 Spotlight) tested OOD generalization to a single held-out domain (New Foundations set theory, 961 pairs), but no work has performed systematic multi-domain rotation evaluation across ≥4 mathematical subdomain categories. We hypothesize that Mathlib module paths (formalization-level structure) and problem-level domain labels (mathematical topic) capture complementary information — a number theory problem may require analysis-level typeclasses — and combining both signals for dynamic retrieval conditioning can close the semantic correctness domain gap that static category context alone cannot address.",
  "landscape": "Current SOTA autoformalization systems — StepFun-Formalizer (40.5% BEq@1 on FormalMATH-Lite, AAAI 2026), ATLAS (NeurIPS 2025), FormaRL (COLM 2025), ProofBridge (+31.14% semantic correctness, ICLR 2026) — all report aggregate metrics with no domain conditioning. Retrieval-augmented approaches are sophisticated but domain-agnostic: DDR (ICLR 2025 Spotlight) introduced ConNF (961 OOD pairs from one domain); CRAMF (ICLR 2026) disambiguates polysemous concepts via contextual query augmentation (concept-level); DRIFT (ICLR 2026) decomposes statements into ~5.8 atomic sub-queries (concept-level decomposition); LeanSearch v2 (May 2026) achieves SOTA premise retrieval (nDCG@10 = 0.623) via hierarchy-informed informalization. None conditions retrieval ranking on the inferred mathematical subdomain of the input problem. In the broader Lean proving ecosystem, LeanPremise/LeanHammer (ICLR 2026; arXiv 2506.07477) provides the first end-to-end domain-general hammer for Lean, achieving strong average OOD performance (20.7% proof rate on miniCTX-v2, 79.4% relative to 26.1% upper bound) via an 82M-parameter neural premise selector with dynamic user-context adaptation — substantially outperforming ReProver (218M params). However, LeanHammer reveals significant project-level variation: Carleson 0%, ConNF 16%, Foundation 38%, FLT 36.4% — confirming that domain-specific challenges persist even in state-of-the-art systems. Critically, LeanHammer targets premise selection for tactic-based PROVING, not autoformalization retrieval, and uses no mathematical subdomain conditioning. KELPS (ICML 2025 AI4Math Workshop; arXiv 2507.08665) achieves 88.9% syntactic accuracy (pass@1) on MiniF2F — outperforming DeepSeek-V3 (81%) and Herald (81.3%) — via Knowledge Equations as an intermediate representation enabling verified multi-language autoformalization (NL → KE → Lean/Coq/Isabelle) across 60k+ NL-FL pairs spanning 6 math topics. KELPS is entirely domain-agnostic with no subdomain conditioning. Aria (ICLR 2026) achieves 42.9% on homological conjectures while all baselines score 0% — the strongest peer-reviewed evidence that domain-agnostic approaches catastrophically fail on specialized subdomains — yet Aria itself uses no domain conditioning. Domain bias is well-documented: MSC-180 found CV values 4–6× above high-variability thresholds across 60 branches; FormalMATH showed 50% algebra vs. 0% discrete math for Goedel-Prover. Domain-stratified performance has been observed: Shebzukhov (2026; arXiv 2603.24372) reports cycle consistency scores ranging from 0.722 (number theory) to 0.516 (calculus) on FineLeanCorpus and 0.641 (abstract algebra) to 0.493 (analysis) on PutnamBench — confirming domain-dependent variation in autoformalization quality — but performs only observational analysis with no domain conditioning, no error type classification, and concludes that 'improvement is general rather than domain-specific.' Limited domain awareness exists in prior work: IndiMathBench (Biyani et al., 2025; arXiv 2512.00997) uses static category-specific Mathlib context blocks achieving 77.9% compilation for Claude Opus 4 but only 17.3% BEq (54/312) with persistent geometry bias (12/98 BEq among top models) — demonstrating that static domain awareness helps compilation but not semantic correctness. SITA (AAAI 2026) applies structure-to-instance formalization for a single domain (optimization). M2F (Feb 2026) and Gloeckle et al. (Apr 2026) formalize entire textbooks in specific domains but use uniform methods. Repair approaches (APRIL, ReForm) apply uniform strategies regardless of domain; notably, APRIL's dataset already contains an 'error_type' field with mutation categories (lme/mlme/thme/tme) and a raw 'error' field with Lean compiler messages, but neither APRIL nor any subsequent work has cross-tabulated these error categories by mathematical subdomain using the dataset's own 'path' field. The community is converging on domain-stratified evaluation: the ICML 2026 AI4Math Workshop offers both ShadowBench (Track 4: end-to-end autoformalization across 8 mathematical areas with semantic alignment pass rate) and FormalRx (Track 1: semantic alignment evaluation using the 28-category SCI Error Taxonomy); Mensfelt et al. (AAAI 2026) propose a common autoformalization framework spanning math, planning, and logic. No prior work provides a systematic domain-stratified cross-tabulation of existing error categories (like APRIL's lme/mlme/thme/tme) combined with a finer-grained error taxonomy extracted from raw compiler messages, characterizing how autoformalization failure types (typeclass failures, coercion mismatches, tactic incompatibilities) distribute differently across mathematical subdomains, nor performs systematic multi-domain rotation evaluation (leave-one-domain-out across ≥5 categories).",
  "inspired_by": "Field gaps #1 (no system conditions dynamic retrieval ranking on inferred mathematical subdomain — IndiMathBench uses static category context, CRAMF disambiguates polysemous concepts, DRIFT decomposes statements into concept-level sub-queries, LeanSearch v2 achieves SOTA domain-agnostic retrieval, LeanPremise/LeanHammer achieves strong domain-general premise selection for proving but with significant project-level variation (Carleson 0% to Foundation 38%) and no subdomain conditioning, but none dynamically conditions reranking on per-problem inferred subdomain for autoformalization), #2 (APRIL 260k tuples with explicit module paths and existing error_type field (lme/mlme/thme/tme) plus raw compiler error messages never cross-tabulated by mathematical subdomain — Shebzukhov (2026) shows domain-stratified aggregate scores but no domain-stratified error type analysis exists), #3 (CRAMF module paths and FineLeanCorpus topic labels never combined for subdomain-conditioned retrieval), #4 (ConNF tests single-domain OOD but no systematic multi-domain rotation exists); innovation patterns 'Retrieval at the Right Abstraction Level' (concept-level decomposition vs. problem-level domain signals) and 'Complementary Label Fusion'; untried combinations #1 (problem-level domain-conditioned retrieval extending CRAMF with APRIL module paths + FineLeanCorpus topic labels) and #2 (domain-stratified cross-tabulation of APRIL's existing error_type categories + finer-grained taxonomy from raw compiler errors as hypothesis-driven analysis); peer-reviewed evidence from Aria (42.9% vs. 0% homological conjectures, ICLR 2026) and MSC-180 (CV 4–6× thresholds across 60 branches) as primary motivation that domain-agnostic approaches systematically fail; LeanPremise/LeanHammer (ICLR 2026) as evidence that domain-dependent difficulty persists even in SOTA Lean premise selection (project variation: 0%–38%), relevant as domain-general retrieval/selection approach in the Lean ecosystem; KELPS (ICML 2025 AI4Math Workshop) as strong domain-agnostic MiniF2F baseline (88.9% pass@1) demonstrating high syntactic accuracy is achievable without domain conditioning, raising the bar for our domain-conditioned approach to demonstrate semantic correctness gains beyond syntactic compilation; Shebzukhov (2026) as corroborating observational evidence of domain-dependent autoformalization quality; IndiMathBench's syntactic-vs-semantic gap (77.9% compilation but 17.3% BEq with persistent geometry bias) as evidence that static domain context solves compilation but not semantic correctness; ShadowBench (ICML 2026 AI4Math Track 4) validating community interest in multi-domain autoformalization evaluation and FormalRx (Track 1) with its SCI Error Taxonomy validating interest in error characterization; contrast with single-domain approaches (SITA, M2F, 130k Topology, Gloeckle et al.) demonstrating domain-specific formalization is tractable but offering no systematic multi-domain conditioning; reviewer preferences for surgical ablations including IndiMathBench-style naive domain prompting baseline, compute-efficient designs, and LeanSearch v2 as strong domain-agnostic retrieval baseline.",
  "approach": "We build a three-stage domain-adaptive autoformalization pipeline on a Goedel-Formalizer-V2-8B backbone (fine-tuned from Qwen3-8B; chosen over the user-specified Qwen2.5-7B because Goedel-Formalizer-V2 is the current SOTA open-source formalizer at this scale, specifically trained for NL→Lean4 translation, and Qwen3-8B provides improved reasoning over Qwen2.5 at comparable parameter count; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct retained as additional baseline for FormaRL comparison). **Stage 1 — Domain-Stratified Error Taxonomy (PRIMARY CONTRIBUTION)**: We leverage APRIL's 260k repair tuples, which include an explicit 'path' field encoding Mathlib module paths per tuple, an existing 'error_type' field with mutation categories (lme: line mutation errors, mlme: multi-line mutation errors, thme: theorem substitution errors comprising 59.5% of the dataset, tme: tactic mutation errors), and a raw 'error' field containing Lean compiler messages (e.g., 'type mismatch', 'unknown constant', 'tactic rewrite failed', 'unsolved goals', 'application type mismatch'). We cluster the 'path' values into 5 major subdomain categories (algebra/ring theory, topology/order, analysis/calculus, number theory/combinatorics, logic/foundations). Our taxonomy contribution is twofold and builds on APRIL's existing categorization rather than constructing error categories from scratch: (i) a domain-stratified cross-tabulation of APRIL's existing error_type categories (lme/mlme/thme/tme) by mathematical subdomain, testing whether mutation category distributions vary significantly across domains (e.g., whether topology has disproportionately more tactic mutation errors while algebra has more line mutation errors); (ii) a finer-grained error taxonomy extracted from the raw 'error' field by parsing Lean compiler messages into semantic categories — typeclass resolution failures, coercion mismatches, tactic incompatibilities, unknown identifier errors, type unification failures, etc. — also stratified by subdomain. The novelty is in the domain stratification and statistical analysis (JSD, predictive power), not in inventing error categories de novo. We cross-reference with FineLeanCorpus's 286k verified entries (which provide hierarchical problem-level domain labels) and Herald's 580k NL-formal pairs (where module paths are recovered by parsing qualified theorem names from formal statements, e.g., extracting 'Topology.Basic' from 'Topology.Basic.isOpen_compl' — an engineering step requiring ~1 additional week beyond direct field access) to measure correlation and divergence between mathematical topic labels, formalization-level module paths, and error patterns. This goes beyond Shebzukhov (2026; arXiv 2603.24372), who reports domain-stratified aggregate cycle consistency scores (number theory 0.722 vs. calculus 0.516) but performs only observational analysis without classifying error categories per domain. **Quantitative success criteria for the error taxonomy** (testable hypotheses that define what constitutes a meaningful finding): (a) **Inter-domain error distribution divergence** — we hypothesize that Jensen-Shannon divergence between error-type distributions across domain pairs will exceed 0.3 (on a [0,1] scale) for at least 3 of 10 domain pairs (e.g., topology vs. algebra, analysis vs. logic), vs. JSD < 0.1 under random domain assignment permutation tests (1000 permutations). Rationale: topology formalizations disproportionately encounter typeclass instance resolution failures (Lean's typeclass system is heavily used for topological spaces, filters, and uniform structures) while algebra formalizations disproportionately encounter coercion chain incompleteness — if these patterns hold, the distributions will diverge substantially. (b) **Predictive power** — we hypothesize that a simple classifier trained on domain → error-type distributions will achieve ≥70% accuracy in predicting the dominant error type for held-out formalizations from a given domain, vs. ~20% baseline (assuming ~5 major error categories). This would demonstrate that knowing a problem's mathematical subdomain provides actionable information about likely failure modes — a qualitative step beyond the aggregate performance differences shown in Shebzukhov (2026). (c) **Actionable recommendations per domain** — for each of the 5 subdomain clusters, we produce a ranked list of the top-5 most frequent error types with concrete mitigation strategies (e.g., 'topology formalizations: prioritize typeclass instance search depth; algebra formalizations: check coercion chain completeness'), evaluated by whether prompting with these recommendations improves formalization accuracy by ≥5 percentage points on held-out examples from that domain vs. prompting without domain-specific error context. If hypotheses (a) and (b) hold, the taxonomy provides the first empirical evidence that autoformalization error types are systematically structured by mathematical subdomain — a finding valuable independent of any downstream pipeline delta, offering actionable guidance for all future domain-specific approaches. The FormalRx challenge (ICML 2026 AI4Math Workshop Track 1) provides a complementary 28-category SCI Error Taxonomy that classifies errors by type alone; our taxonomy is orthogonal in that it stratifies errors by mathematical subdomain, and the two taxonomies can be cross-referenced to test whether certain SCI error categories correlate with specific subdomains. ShadowBench (Track 4 of the same workshop) evaluates end-to-end autoformalization across 8 mathematical areas but does not classify error types. If the hypotheses do not hold (JSD < 0.15 across all domain pairs, prediction accuracy < 40%), we report this as a meaningful negative result: autoformalization errors are domain-invariant, and domain-adaptive approaches should focus on retrieval rather than error-aware prompting. **Stage 2 — Domain-Conditioned Retrieval**: We extend CRAMF's dual-channel hybrid retrieval with a domain-aware reranking layer that boosts same-subdomain definitions. This operates at a fundamentally different level than existing retrieval innovations: CRAMF disambiguates polysemous concepts (concept-level); DRIFT decomposes statements into atomic sub-queries (concept-level decomposition); LeanSearch v2 achieves SOTA domain-agnostic retrieval (retrieval quality); LeanPremise/LeanHammer achieves strong domain-general premise selection for proving (not autoformalization); IndiMathBench provides static category context (static domain awareness). Our reranker adds an orthogonal signal: given that the input problem is dynamically classified as topology, boost ALL topology-related definitions in retrieval, not just disambiguate individual concepts, decompose the statement, or apply a static category context block. The reranker operates per-problem (not per-category), using the inferred subdomain to weight retrieval results dynamically. The domain classifier for retrieval conditioning uses APRIL's explicit path field as primary training signal, supplemented by Herald's parsed module paths and FineLeanCorpus topic labels. The reranker is trained on this combined data with domain match as an additional feature alongside the existing semantic similarity score. We compare domain-conditioned retrieval vs. domain-agnostic retrieval at matched retrieval budget (same Top-K, same compute) to isolate the domain signal's contribution. We additionally compare against LeanSearch v2's standard mode as a strong domain-agnostic retrieval baseline. **Stage 3 — Domain-Aware Autoformalization**: Using Goedel-Formalizer-V2-8B, we apply domain-prefixed prompting: the input is augmented with predicted subdomain label, top domain-specific error patterns from Stage 1, and domain-conditioned retrieved definitions from Stage 2. We perform LoRA fine-tuning (rank 32) on domain-enriched data combining Herald and FineLeanCorpus, where each training example includes its domain context. No complex LoRA routing or domain-specific adapters — a single adapter learns to use domain context from the prompt. **Evaluation**: We introduce the first systematic multi-domain rotation evaluation protocol for autoformalization — leave-one-domain-out across our 5 subdomain categories, extending ConNF's single-domain OOD paradigm to systematic cross-domain generalization testing. Evaluated on FormalMATH-categorized problems and MathAtlas's 87-area benchmark. MSC-180's 60-branch classification serves as cross-domain generalization test. ConNF serves as an additional single-domain OOD test (New Foundations set theory). We position our evaluation protocol relative to ShadowBench (Track 4): while ShadowBench evaluates across 8 mathematical areas with fixed splits, our leave-one-domain-out rotation provides systematic cross-domain generalization measurement that fixed-split evaluation cannot. Surgical ablations isolate: (a) domain-conditioned retrieval alone (Stage 2 only), (b) domain-prefixed prompting alone (subdomain label in prompt, no retrieval change), (c) domain error context alone (error patterns in prompt, no retrieval change), (d) full combination (Stages 1+2+3), (e) **IndiMathBench-style naive domain prompting baseline** — prepending static category-specific Mathlib context to the input, replicating IndiMathBench's category-based retrieval approach at inference time; this tests whether the simple static approach that dramatically improves compilation also closes the semantic correctness gap, and (f) **LeanSearch v2 retrieval baseline** — replacing our domain-conditioned retrieval with LeanSearch v2's standard mode to test whether superior domain-agnostic retrieval subsumes domain conditioning. If ablation (e) captures 80%+ of semantic correctness gains, we report this honestly as evidence that the simple approach extends to semantic correctness — a valuable finding in itself; if the full pipeline significantly outperforms, it validates the engineering investment in dynamic conditioning and error taxonomy. A domain-agnostic matched-compute baseline (same LoRA budget, same retrieval budget, no domain conditioning) serves as control. Per-domain improvement analysis focuses on whether currently weak domains (analysis, discrete math, topology, geometry) show disproportionate gains. Domain-conditioned retrieval HitRate@K metrics provide pipeline-internal evaluation independent of downstream formalization accuracy.",

You are revising a research idea based on reviewer feedback.

## Original idea
{
  "title": "Domain-Adaptive Autoformalization via Subdomain-Conditioned Retrieval and Error Taxonomy",
  "core_problem": "Current autoformalization systems treat all mathematical subdomains identically, yet empirical evidence from MSC-180 (CV values 4–6× above high-variability thresholds across 60 mathematical branches) and FormalMATH (0% on discrete math vs. 50% on algebra for Goedel-Prover) reveals severe, systematic domain bias. Aria (ICLR 2026) independently confirms this: 42.9% on homological conjectures while all baselines (Gemini-2.5-Pro, Goedel-Formalizer-V2-32B, Kimina-Autoformalizer-7B) achieve 0% — demonstrating that certain specialized domains are catastrophically underserved even by SOTA systems. Shebzukhov (2026; arXiv 2603.24372) provides complementary evidence via cycle consistency fine-tuning on FineLeanCorpus: number theory achieves 0.722 cycle consistency vs. calculus at 0.516, confirming domain-dependent performance variation — but this observational analysis reports only aggregate performance per domain without analyzing how error types differ across subdomains. IndiMathBench (Biyani et al., 2025; arXiv 2512.00997) provides further corroboration: static category-specific Mathlib context boosts syntactic compilation rates dramatically (e.g., Claude Opus 4: 4.1% → 77.9%) but BEq semantic correctness is only 17.3% (54/312 problems) and deeply domain-biased — only 12 of 98 geometry problems achieve BEq success among top models vs. far higher rates for algebra and number theory — demonstrating that even rudimentary domain awareness improves compilation but the harder semantic correctness gap persists with clear domain structure. Meanwhile, retrieval-augmented approaches address retrieval quality through increasingly sophisticated methods — CRAMF uses contextual query augmentation for concept-level disambiguation, DRIFT (ICLR 2026) decomposes statements into ~5.8 atomic sub-queries for targeted concept-level retrieval, LeanSearch v2 (May 2026) achieves SOTA premise retrieval (nDCG@10 = 0.623) without any domain-specific fine-tuning via hierarchy-informed informalization, and LeanPremise/LeanHammer (ICLR 2026; arXiv 2506.07477) achieves 79.4% relative proof rate on OOD benchmarks via neural premise selection for Lean proving — but none conditions retrieval ranking on the inferred mathematical subdomain of the input problem in a dynamic, per-problem fashion for autoformalization. The 260k repair tuples in APRIL contain an explicit 'error_type' field encoding mutation categories (lme: line mutation errors, mlme: multi-line mutation errors, thme: theorem substitution errors, tme: tactic mutation errors) and an 'error' field with raw Lean compiler messages (e.g., 'type mismatch', 'unknown constant', 'tactic rewrite failed', 'unsolved goals'), but these have never been cross-tabulated by mathematical subdomain despite the dataset containing explicit Mathlib module paths in each tuple's 'path' field. Can we build the first autoformalization pipeline that systematically conditions its dynamic retrieval ranking and prompting signals on inferred mathematical subdomain — beyond both static category context (IndiMathBench) and concept-level disambiguation/decomposition (CRAMF/DRIFT) — and can we provide the first domain-stratified cross-tabulation of APRIL's existing error categories plus a finer-grained error taxonomy extracted from raw Lean compiler messages, characterizing how autoformalization error TYPES distribute across mathematical subdomains with statistical rigor, going beyond observational domain-stratified scores (Shebzukhov, 2026)?",
  "opportunity": "Six critical resources and findings converged in 2025–2026 that make domain-adaptive autoformalization both feasible and necessary, each containing underexploited domain metadata: (1) Herald (ICLR 2025) provides 580k NL-formal pairs where Mathlib4 module paths can be recovered by parsing qualified theorem names from formal statements (e.g., extracting 'Topology.Basic' from theorem names like 'Topology.Basic.isOpen_compl') — the released HuggingFace dataset (FrenzyMath/Herald_statements) contains id, informal_statement, and formal_statement fields without an explicit module path column, requiring parsing or re-running the Lean-Jixia extraction pipeline; (2) FineLeanCorpus/CriticLean (2025) provides 286k verified entries (509k total) with hierarchical problem-level domain labels and difficulty scores — but these capture mathematical topic, not formalization-level structure; (3) APRIL (Feb 2026) provides 260k repair tuples (59.5% theorem substitution errors, plus tactic, multi-line, and line mutations) with an explicit 'path' field encoding Mathlib module paths per tuple AND an existing 'error_type' field classifying mutation categories (lme/mlme/thme/tme) plus a raw 'error' field containing Lean compiler messages — making it the most immediately usable source for domain-stratified error analysis, as module paths can be directly mapped to mathematical subdomains without additional parsing, and our taxonomy contribution builds on APRIL's existing error categorization by cross-tabulating these mutation categories with mathematical subdomain and constructing a finer-grained taxonomy from the raw compiler error messages (parsing semantic categories such as typeclass resolution failures, coercion mismatches, tactic incompatibilities from raw strings like 'type mismatch', 'unknown constant', 'unsolved goals'); (4) CRAMF's 26k-definition knowledge base stores module paths (θ_p) per definition and uses LLM-generated contextual query augmentation to disambiguate polysemous concepts, but never conditions its retrieval reranking (bge-reranker-v2-m3) on the mathematical subdomain of the input problem; (5) MathAtlas (May 2026) provides 52k entities across 87 math areas with 178k dependency relations, using domain labels only for evaluation not pipeline conditioning; (6) LeanSearch v2 (May 2026) achieves SOTA domain-agnostic premise retrieval via hierarchy-informed Mathlib informalization — but its success demonstrates that retrieval quality alone does not address the domain bias problem documented by MSC-180 and FormalMATH, because domain bias manifests in formalization accuracy, not retrieval recall; and (7) IndiMathBench (Biyani et al., 2025; arXiv 2512.00997) demonstrates that static category-specific Mathlib context dramatically improves compilation rates for 4 mathematical domains — proving domain awareness helps — but uses one-time static context blocks with human-labeled categories rather than dynamic per-problem conditioning, and its BEq results (17.3% for Claude Opus 4, 54/312) reveal a persistent syntactic-vs-semantic gap with strong domain bias (geometry: 12/98 BEq among top models), leaving the semantic correctness challenge unaddressed. Note: IndiMathBench is an arXiv preprint (desk-rejected from ICLR 2026); its compilation and domain-bias patterns are corroborated by peer-reviewed evidence from MSC-180, FormalMATH, and Aria. Crucially, MSC-180 (Dec 2025) quantified domain bias with coefficient of variation metrics across 60 mathematical branches showing best models achieve only 18.89% overall with maximum 41.7% domain coverage, FormalMATH (2025) showed Goedel-Prover achieving 50% on algebra but 0% on discrete math, and Aria's homological conjectures results (42.9% vs. 0% for all baselines) provide the strongest peer-reviewed evidence that domain-specialized problems require fundamentally different handling. Shebzukhov (2026; arXiv 2603.24372) corroborates domain performance variation via cycle consistency fine-tuning — number theory at 0.722 vs. calculus at 0.516 — but performs only post-hoc observational analysis with no domain conditioning or error type classification. LeanPremise/LeanHammer (ICLR 2026; arXiv 2506.07477) provides further evidence of domain-dependent difficulty in the Lean ecosystem: its neural premise selection achieves strong average OOD performance (20.7% on miniCTX-v2) but with dramatic project-level variation (Carleson 0%, Foundation 38%, ConNF 16%, FLT 36.4%), confirming that domain-specific challenges persist even for state-of-the-art retrieval/selection systems — though LeanHammer targets proving (premise selection for tactic-based proof search) rather than autoformalization. KELPS (ICML 2025 AI4Math Workshop; arXiv 2507.08665) achieves 88.9% syntactic accuracy (pass@1) on MiniF2F via Knowledge Equations as intermediate representation, outperforming DeepSeek-V3 (81%) and Herald (81.3%) — but is entirely domain-agnostic with no subdomain conditioning, operating across 6 math topics without analyzing domain-specific error patterns. The ICML 2026 AI4Math Workshop validates growing community interest in domain-aware autoformalization evaluation through two complementary challenge tracks: Track 4 (ShadowBench) evaluates end-to-end autoformalization across 8 mathematical areas with semantic alignment pass rate metrics; Track 1 (FormalRx) evaluates semantic alignment preservation using the FormalRx-Test dataset built on a 28-category SCI Error Taxonomy that classifies errors by type. ConNF (DDR, ICLR 2025 Spotlight) tested OOD generalization to a single held-out domain (New Foundations set theory, 961 pairs), but no work has performed systematic multi-domain rotation evaluation across ≥4 mathematical subdomain categories. We hypothesize that Mathlib module paths (formalization-level structure) and problem-level domain labels (mathematical topic) capture complementary information — a number theory problem may require analysis-level typeclasses — and combining both signals for dynamic retrieval conditioning can close the semantic correctness domain gap that static category context alone cannot address.",
  "landscape": "Current SOTA autoformalization systems — StepFun-Formalizer (40.5% BEq@1 on FormalMATH-Lite, AAAI 2026), ATLAS (NeurIPS 2025), FormaRL (COLM 2025), ProofBridge (+31.14% semantic correctness, ICLR 2026) — all report aggregate metrics with no domain conditioning. Retrieval-augmented approaches are sophisticated but domain-agnostic: DDR (ICLR 2025 Spotlight) introduced ConNF (961 OOD pairs from one domain); CRAMF (ICLR 2026) disambiguates polysemous concepts via contextual query augmentation (concept-level); DRIFT (ICLR 2026) decomposes statements into ~5.8 atomic sub-queries (concept-level decomposition); LeanSearch v2 (May 2026) achieves SOTA premise retrieval (nDCG@10 = 0.623) via hierarchy-informed informalization. None conditions retrieval ranking on the inferred mathematical subdomain of the input problem. In the broader Lean proving ecosystem, LeanPremise/LeanHammer (ICLR 2026; arXiv 2506.07477) provides the first end-to-end domain-general hammer for Lean, achieving strong average OOD performance (20.7% proof rate on miniCTX-v2, 79.4% relative to 26.1% upper bound) via an 82M-parameter neural premise selector with dynamic user-context adaptation — substantially outperforming ReProver (218M params). However, LeanHammer reveals significant project-level variation: Carleson 0%, ConNF 16%, Foundation 38%, FLT 36.4% — confirming that domain-specific challenges persist even in state-of-the-art systems. Critically, LeanHammer targets premise selection for tactic-based PROVING, not autoformalization retrieval, and uses no mathematical subdomain conditioning. KELPS (ICML 2025 AI4Math Workshop; arXiv 2507.08665) achieves 88.9% syntactic accuracy (pass@1) on MiniF2F — outperforming DeepSeek-V3 (81%) and Herald (81.3%) — via Knowledge Equations as an intermediate representation enabling verified multi-language autoformalization (NL → KE → Lean/Coq/Isabelle) across 60k+ NL-FL pairs spanning 6 math topics. KELPS is entirely domain-agnostic with no subdomain conditioning. Aria (ICLR 2026) achieves 42.9% on homological conjectures while all baselines score 0% — the strongest peer-reviewed evidence that domain-agnostic approaches catastrophically fail on specialized subdomains — yet Aria itself uses no domain conditioning. Domain bias is well-documented: MSC-180 found CV values 4–6× above high-variability thresholds across 60 branches; FormalMATH showed 50% algebra vs. 0% discrete math for Goedel-Prover. Domain-stratified performance has been observed: Shebzukhov (2026; arXiv 2603.24372) reports cycle consistency scores ranging from 0.722 (number theory) to 0.516 (calculus) on FineLeanCorpus and 0.641 (abstract algebra) to 0.493 (analysis) on PutnamBench — confirming domain-dependent variation in autoformalization quality — but performs only observational analysis with no domain conditioning, no error type classification, and concludes that 'improvement is general rather than domain-specific.' Limited domain awareness exists in prior work: IndiMathBench (Biyani et al., 2025; arXiv 2512.00997) uses static category-specific Mathlib context blocks achieving 77.9% compilation for Claude Opus 4 but only 17.3% BEq (54/312) with persistent geometry bias (12/98 BEq among top models) — demonstrating that static domain awareness helps compilation but not semantic correctness. SITA (AAAI 2026) applies structure-to-instance formalization for a single domain (optimization). M2F (Feb 2026) and Gloeckle et al. (Apr 2026) formalize entire textbooks in specific domains but use uniform methods. Repair approaches (APRIL, ReForm) apply uniform strategies regardless of domain; notably, APRIL's dataset already contains an 'error_type' field with mutation categories (lme/mlme/thme/tme) and a raw 'error' field with Lean compiler messages, but neither APRIL nor any subsequent work has cross-tabulated these error categories by mathematical subdomain using the dataset's own 'path' field. The reranker operates per-problem (not per-category), using the inferred subdomain to weight retrieval results dynamically. Based on the search results, I found the paper you're looking for. Here's information about the arXiv paper 2604.19459:

## Paper Overview

The paper "Do LLMs Game Formalization? Evaluating Faithfulness in Logical Reasoning" by Kyuhee Kim, Auguste Poiroux, and Antoine Bosselut investigates whether frontier models exploit the gap between valid proofs and faithful translations when generating Lean 4 proofs, a behavior termed formalization gaming.

## Key Concepts

A formalization is faithful if the formal axioms preserve the semantic content of the natural language premises. Valid proofs and faithful formalizations are independent properties, and a valid proof may rest on an unfaithful formalization.

## Methodology

The researchers evaluated GPT-5 and DeepSeek-R1 on 303 first-order logic problems (203 from FOLIO, 100 from Multi-LogiEval), comparing unified generation against a two-stage pipeline that separates formalization from proving.

## Key Findings

Despite compilation rates of 87–99%, the researchers found no evidence of systematic gaming in unified generation: models prefer reporting failure over forcing proofs, even under prompting designed to encourage it. However, the two-stage pipeline reveals two distinct modes of unfaithfulness: GPT-5 fabricates axioms during proof generation, while DeepSeek-R1 mistranslates premises during formalization, producing internally consistent outputs that evade detection entirely.

# Paper Analysis: Do LLMs Game Formalization?

## Core Details

**Title:** Do LLMs Game Formalization? Evaluating Faithfulness in Logical Reasoning

**Authors:** Kyuhee Kim, Auguste Poiroux, Antoine Bosselut

**Venue:** VerifAI-2 Workshop, ICLR 2026 (non-archival)

**Submission Date:** April 21, 2026

## Key Contributions

The paper investigates whether large language models exploit gaps between valid proofs and faithful formalizations when generating Lean 4 proofs. The researchers introduce the concept of "formalization gaming" to describe this behavior.

## Methodology & Dataset

- **Models tested:** GPT-5 and DeepSeek-R1
- **Dataset size:** 303 first-order logic problems (203 from FOLIO, 100 from Multi-LogiEval)
- **Approach:** Compared unified generation against a two-stage pipeline separating formalization from proof generation
- **Compilation success rates:** 87-99%

## Key Findings on Semantic Faithfulness

The study identifies two distinct unfaithfulness modes:

1. **GPT-5 behavior:** Fabricates axioms during proof generation; detectable through cross-stage comparison
2. **DeepSeek-R1 behavior:** Mistranslates premises during formalization, producing "internally consistent outputs that evade detection entirely"

Notably, models prefer reporting failure over forcing proofs, showing limited systematic gaming despite high compilation rates.

## Error Taxonomy

The abstract mentions the gap between valid proofs and faithful translations but does not explicitly detail named error categories (mistranslation, fabrication, omission, contradiction) as separate taxonomy definitions in the provided content.

# Error Taxonomy and Analysis from "Do LLMs Game Formalization?"

## Error Categories

The paper organizes formalization errors into four main categories:

1. **Mistranslation** (8 subtypes): Wrong connective, negation, quantifier, direction, scope, predicate, entity, or argument order
2. **Fabrication** (2 subtypes): Fabricated axioms or conclusion-as-axiom
3. **Omission** (2 subtypes): Missing axioms or dropped antecedents
4. **Contradiction**: Induced contradictions enabling logical explosion

## Error Definitions

Per Table 1, examples include:
- "Wrong connective: P∧Q for P→Q"
- "Conclusion as axiom: Goal stated as axiom"
- "Missing axiom: Premise not formalized"

## Frequency Data

Among **prediction errors** (n=124 unified approach cases):
- 77% involved **faithful formalization** (errors despite correct translation)
- 23% were **unfaithful** (stemming from translation failures)

In **two-stage modifications** (GPT-5, n=105):
- 56% conclusion-as-axiom
- 16% world knowledge
- 12% invented axioms
- 11% contradictions

## Post-Compilation Analysis

This taxonomy specifically targets **post-compilation semantic errors**. The paper emphasizes: "Formal verification provides strong guarantees for the latter: a proof that type-checks in Lean's kernel is mathematically valid. However, verification reveals nothing about whether the formalization faithfully represents the original natural language."

## Relationship to Autoformalization

The authors synthesize prior taxonomies from Barker-Plummer et al. (2008) and Thatikonda et al. (2024), but extend them: "Our multi-statement setting introduces additional possibilities. Models may fabricate axioms absent from premises, omit premises entirely, or induce contradictions."

# CAM-Bench: Computational and Applied Mathematics Formalization

## Title and Authors
**Title:** "CAM-Bench: A Benchmark for Computational and Applied Mathematics in Lean"

**Authors:** Wentao Long, Yunfei Li, Chenyi Li, Li Zhou, Chumin Sun, and Zaiwen Wen

## Key Contributions

The paper introduces a formal theorem-proving benchmark addressing a significant gap in existing evaluation resources. The authors developed a specialized collection targeting applied mathematics rather than the Olympiad-style problems that dominate current benchmarks.

## Benchmark Scale and Scope

The benchmark comprises **1,000 Lean proof targets** spanning three mathematical domains:
- Optimization
- Numerical linear algebra
- Numerical analysis

Problems were adapted from textbook exercises that often depend on locally introduced concepts and elementary results not standardized in Mathlib4.

## Construction Methodology

The team developed a "dependency-recovery pipeline" to reconstruct local textbook context for each problem. The process involved:

1. Recovering contextual material from source materials
2. Normalizing problems into standalone informal theorems
3. Translating these into Lean 4 targets
4. Validating through compilation and semantic review

This approach ensures problems remain faithful to their original formulations while functioning as independent proof targets.

## Evaluation Findings

The paper identifies critical failure modes in how language models and formalization agents handle these problems:

- Tracking assumptions introduced locally
- Applying elementary results appropriately
- Decomposing complex proofs
- Maintaining control across extended Lean proofs

These findings suggest domain-specific challenges in computational mathematics formalization differ from pure algebra or logic domains.

content.content:
# CAM-Bench Evaluation Results and Domain Analysis

## Models Tested and Overall Performance

The paper evaluated several frontier language models on CAM-Bench:

- **Deepseek-v4-pro**: 19.67% verified Lean accuracy (pass@32)
- **Claude-sonnet-4.6**: 19.28% verified Lean accuracy
- **Gemini-3.1-pro-preview**: 18.38% verified Lean accuracy
- **GPT-5.4**: 11.70% (pass@32), improving to 44.00% with agentic repair
- **Kimi-k2.6**: 2.25% verified Lean accuracy

## Domain-Specific Breakdown

The benchmark contains **1,000 Lean proof targets** organized into six reasoning categories:

1. Spectral and matrix reasoning
2. Convexity and geometric inequalities
3. Optimization modeling and duality
4. Optimality conditions and constrained quadratic reasoning
5. Algorithms and convergence
6. Applied modeling (robust, statistical, inverse, network optimization)

**However, the paper does not provide granular per-domain performance metrics** breaking down model accuracy across these six categories or the three primary mathematical areas (optimization, numerical linear algebra, numerical analysis).

## Key Performance Gap

A significant informal-formal gap emerged: pass@1 informal accuracy ranged from 70.0%-83.8%, yet verified Lean accuracy remained below 20% for non-agentic baselines, indicating models struggled with Lean syntax, Mathlib conventions, and formal verification requirements.

## Agentic Systems Comparison

External agentic provers showed substantially better performance on a 200-instance sample:
- **M2F**: 71.5% solved (143/200 instances)
- **Aristotle**: 62.5% solved (125/200 instances)

## Dominant Failure Patterns

Error analysis revealed three primary bottlenecks affecting 50.8%-71.5% of failures:
- Library/API grounding issues (72.6% of pass@32 failures)
- Formal representation and type discipline problems (50.8%)
- Proof decomposition and long-horizon control difficulties (71.5%)

The paper does not provide detailed comparisons with MiniF2F or FormalMATH performance metrics.

## Library Structure and Organization

Mathlib4 is a comprehensive, community-maintained library of formalized mathematics for the Lean 4 theorem prover containing over 1000+ formalized theorems spanning algebra, analysis, topology, geometry, number theory, category theory, and other mathematical domains. The mathematical library is structured by domain, with sophisticated hierarchies for algebraic and analytic objects.

## Import Architecture

Virtually all files in the library transitively import Mathlib.Init which establishes the root environment and linter sets.

## Topology Implementation

The TopologicalSpace typeclass is defined in mathlib in Mathlib.Topology.Defs.Basic. The TopologicalSpace typeclass is an inductive type, defined as a structure on a type α with an IsOpen predicate and the axioms for a topology.

## Cross-Domain Dependencies

An example of cross-domain typeclass interaction appears in the integration of topology and other mathematical structures. Consider the pair MetricSpace / TopologicalSpace and the topology on a product of two metric spaces, which could be obtained by going from each metric space to its topology, then taking the product topology, or by considering the product metric space and then the topology coming from the distance.

## Proof Automation and Tactics

Mathlib provides a massive collection of tactics (over 200) aggregated in Mathlib/Tactic.lean, ranging from decision procedures for specific algebraic structures to general-purpose simplifiers, and includes specialized logic tools such as the Fact typeclass for providing witnesses to the typeclass system.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about cross-domain theorems and formalization challenges in Mathlib:

## Mathlib Cross-Domain Theorems and Challenges

Mathlib4 is a comprehensive, community-maintained library of formalized mathematics for the Lean 4 theorem prover containing over 1000+ formalized theorems spanning algebra, analysis, topology, geometry, number theory, category theory, and other mathematical domains.

### Examples of Cross-Domain Theorems

One prominent example involves the change of variables formula: The formalization of the change of variables formula in integrals builds on developments in linear algebra, analysis, measure theory and descriptive set theory. This theorem mixes several domains of mathematics typically taught in different courses, and can only be formalized in a library developed enough in all these directions with areas that can interact in a coherent way.

Another significant cross-domain effort is Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes. The formalization of the first case of Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes uses Lean and mathlib, an important 19th century result that motivated the development of modern algebraic number theory. The formalization process faced difficulties including dealing with a diamond about characteristic zero fields and problems arising from multiple nested coercions related to number fields.

### Progress in Analytic Number Theory

While Lean's library has lagged behind other theorem provers in certain analytical domains, projects aim to bridge this gap by formalizing important theorems in areas like calculus and analytic number theory to enhance Lean's analytical content in Mathlib.

## Key Findings:

**Precision@K Metric Definition:**
Precision@K measures the proportion of relevant documents in the top K results retrieved by a system. For example, if a search engine returns 3 documents (K=3) and 2 are relevant, precision@3 is 2/3 ≈ 66.7%.

**High Precision and Noise Reduction:**
A high precision@3 ensures the top 3 documents are highly relevant, which is critical for downstream tasks like answer generation. High precision@3 reduces noise and ensures the generator operates on trustworthy data.

**Quality vs. Quantity Trade-off:**
Precision@k largely emphasizes each retrieved result being valid, rather than exhaustively finding each and every result. In other words, Precision@k can serve well as a retrieval measure for scenarios valuing the quality of retrieved results over quantity—retrieving results that we are sure are relevant, even if this means we mistakenly reject some relevant results.

**Domain and Noise Filtering Techniques:**
Information-theoretic methods like IB Filtering use principles from the information bottleneck framework to retain only high-utility input features while discarding noise. Though computation-heavy, IB Filtering improves EM by +3.2 with a 2.5% compression ratio, offering a balance between precision and conciseness.

**Distractor Filtering:**
The Selector serves as a precision-focused filter that removes distractors introduced during retrieval. Large corpora inevitably yield passages that share surface-level words with the query but are semantically off-topic, and passing such noise directly to a QA model leads to error propagation.

## CRAMF Framework Overview

CRAMF is a Concept-driven Retrieval-Augmented Mathematical Formalization framework that enhances formalization accuracy by retrieving precise definitions of core mathematical concepts from Mathlib to provide contextual grounding for LLM-based autoformalizers.

## Retrieval Challenges

Applying retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in this setting is non-trivial due to the lack of structured knowledge bases, the polymorphic nature of mathematical concepts, and the high precision required in formal retrieval. Additionally, resolving conceptual polymorphism requires not just retrieving related content, but disambiguating between multiple context-sensitive formalizations, a task that standard RAG pipelines are not equipped to handle.

## Technical Solutions

To address these challenges, CRAMF implements several key components:

1. **Knowledge Base**: The framework automatically constructs a concept-definition knowledge base from Mathlib4, the standard mathematical library for the Lean 4 theorem prover, indexing over 26,000 formal definitions and 1,000+ core mathematical concepts.

2. **Query Augmentation**: To address conceptual polymorphism, CRAMF proposes contextual query augmentation with domain- and application-level signals.

3. **Hybrid Retrieval Strategy**: CRAMF designs a dual-channel hybrid retrieval strategy with reranking to ensure accurate and relevant definition retrieval.

These mechanisms are specifically designed to handle the noise and irrelevant definitions that can degrade retrieval performance when K is high, through domain-aware filtering and context-sensitive disambiguation.

# CRAMF Retrieval Analysis: Precision, Domain Handling, and Limitations

## 1. Retrieval Precision as K Increases

The paper provides **HitRate@K analysis only at K=3**, not a comprehensive degradation study. Table 4 shows CRAMF achieves 44.2% HitRate@3 on miniF2F, but there's no precision@K curve showing how performance decays at higher K values. The framework focuses on "Top-3 definitions with the highest semantic match" for final selection, suggesting deliberate limitation rather than comprehensive precision analysis across multiple thresholds.

## 2. Cross-Domain Problem Handling

The paper does **not explicitly address cross-domain scenarios**. While AdvancedMath covers "spatial analytic geometry, vector algebra, series theory, and ordinary differential equations," there's no discussion of problems requiring simultaneous topology and number theory concepts, or similar multi-domain challenges.

## 3. Contextual Query Augmentation Scope

Query enhancement uses **both concept and contextual interpretation**:

> "The concept is then concatenated with this terminological interpretation to form the query...domain information and application context for the concept"

However, the paper doesn't clarify whether "domain information" means explicit subdomain classification or emerges implicitly from the theorem description's language.

## 4. Domain Coverage Limitations

The paper provides **minimal discussion of limitations**. It mentions the knowledge base covers "1,000+ core mathematical concepts" from Mathlib4 but doesn't specify which domains remain underrepresented or excluded.

## 5. Multi-Domain Boundary Problems

**No analysis exists** for problems requiring knowledge at disciplinary intersections. The ablation study and case studies focus on single-concept scenarios rather than multi-domain entanglement challenges.

Shebzukhov (2026; arXiv 2603.24372) provides complementary evidence via cycle consistency fine-tuning on FineLeanCorpus: number theory achieves 0.722 cycle consistency vs. calculus at 0.516, confirming domain-dependent performance variation — but this observational analysis reports only aggregate performance per domain without analyzing how error types differ across subdomains. CAM-Bench (Long et al., 2026; arXiv 2605.17255) corroborates domain-specific difficulty from the applied mathematics side: 1,000 Lean proof targets in optimization, numerical linear algebra, and numerical analysis reveal that frontier models achieve less than 20% verified Lean accuracy (non-agentic), with library/API grounding failures accounting for 72.6% of errors — demonstrating that computational and applied math domains present qualitatively different formalization challenges than the algebra and olympiad-style problems dominating existing benchmarks. IndiMathBench (Biyani et al., 2025; arXiv 2512.00997) provides further corroboration: static category-specific Mathlib context boosts syntactic compilation rates dramatically (e.g., Claude Opus 4: 4.1% → 77.9%) but BEq semantic correctness is only 17.3% (54/312 problems) and deeply domain-biased — only 12 of 98 geometry problems achieve BEq success among top models vs. far higher rates for algebra and number theory — demonstrating that even rudimentary domain awareness improves compilation but the harder semantic correctness gap persists with clear domain structure. Meanwhile, retrieval-augmented approaches address retrieval quality through increasingly sophisticated methods — CRAMF uses contextual query augmentation for concept-level disambiguation, DRIFT (ICLR 2026) decomposes statements into ~5.8 atomic sub-queries for targeted concept-level retrieval, LeanSearch v2 (May 2026) achieves SOTA premise retrieval (nDCG@10 = 0.623) without any domain-specific fine-tuning via hierarchy-informed informalization, and LeanPremise/LeanHammer (ICLR 2026; arXiv 2506.07477) achieves 79.4% relative proof rate on OOD benchmarks via neural premise selection for Lean proving — but none conditions retrieval ranking on the inferred mathematical subdomain of the input problem in a dynamic, per-problem fashion for autoformalization.   "opportunity": "Six critical resources and findings converged in 2025–2026 that make domain-adaptive autoformalization both feasible and necessary, each containing underexploited domain metadata: (1) Herald (ICLR 2025) provides 580k NL-formal pairs where Mathlib4 module paths can be recovered by parsing qualified theorem names from formal statements (e.g., extracting 'Topology.Basic' from theorem names like 'Topology.Basic.isOpen_compl') — the released HuggingFace dataset (FrenzyMath/Herald_statements) contains id, informal_statement, and formal_statement fields without an explicit module path column, requiring parsing or re-running the Lean-Jixia extraction pipeline;   "landscape": "Current SOTA autoformalization systems — StepFun-Formalizer (40.5% BEq@1 on FormalMATH-Lite, AAAI 2026), ATLAS (NeurIPS 2025), FormaRL (COLM 2025), ProofBridge (+31.14% semantic correctness, ICLR 2026) — all report aggregate metrics with no domain conditioning. None conditions retrieval ranking on the inferred mathematical subdomain of the input problem. In the broader Lean proving ecosystem, LeanPremise/LeanHammer (ICLR 2026; arXiv 2506.07477) provides the first end-to-end domain-general hammer for Lean, achieving strong average OOD performance (20.7% proof rate on miniCTX-v2, 79.4% relative to 26.1% upper bound) via an 82M-parameter neural premise selector with dynamic user-context adaptation — substantially outperforming ReProver (218M params). However, LeanHammer reveals significant project-level variation: Carleson 0%, ConNF 16%, Foundation 38%, FLT 36.4% — confirming that domain-specific challenges persist even in state-of-the-art systems. Critically, LeanHammer targets premise selection for tactic-based PROVING, not autoformalization retrieval, and uses no mathematical subdomain conditioning. KELPS (ICML 2025 AI4Math Workshop; arXiv 2507.08665) achieves 88.9% syntactic accuracy (pass@1) on MiniF2F — outperforming DeepSeek-V3 (81%) and Herald (81.3%) — via Knowledge Equations as an intermediate representation enabling verified multi-language autoformalization (NL → KE → Lean/Coq/Isabelle) across 60k+ NL-FL pairs spanning 6 math topics. Aria (ICLR 2026) achieves 42.9% on homological conjectures while all baselines score 0% — the strongest peer-reviewed evidence that domain-agnostic approaches catastrophically fail on specialized subdomains — yet Aria itself uses no domain conditioning. Domain-stratified performance has been observed: Shebzukhov (2026; arXiv 2603.24372) reports cycle consistency scores ranging from 0.722 (number theory) to 0.516 (calculus) on FineLeanCorpus and 0.641 (abstract algebra) to 0.493 (analysis) on PutnamBench — confirming domain-dependent variation in autoformalization quality — but performs only observational analysis with no domain conditioning, no error type classification, and concludes that 'improvement is general rather than domain-specific.' (Apr 2026) formalize entire textbooks in specific domains but use uniform methods.   "approach": "We build a three-stage domain-adaptive autoformalization pipeline on a Goedel-Formalizer-V2-8B backbone (fine-tuned from Qwen3-8B; chosen as a competitive open-source formalizer at this scale — StepFun-Formalizer-7B achieves higher BEq@1 on FormalMATH-Lite (38.3% vs. Kimina-7B's 35.1%) and is included as an additional backbone comparison, but Goedel-Formalizer-V2-8B's thinking-augmented generation (reasoning before formalizing) may be particularly beneficial for domain-conditioned prompting where the model must interpret domain context and error patterns before generating formal statements; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct retained as additional baseline for FormaRL comparison). **Stage 1 — Domain-Stratified Error Taxonomy (PRIMARY CONTRIBUTION)**: We leverage APRIL's 260k repair tuples, which include an explicit 'path' field encoding Mathlib module paths per tuple, an existing 'error_type' field with mutation categories (lme: line mutation errors, mlme: multi-line mutation errors, thme: theorem substitution errors comprising 59.5% of the dataset, tme: tactic mutation errors), and a raw 'error' field containing Lean compiler messages (e.g., 'type mismatch', 'unknown constant', 'tactic rewrite failed', 'unsolved goals', 'application type mismatch'). We cluster the 'path' values into 5 major subdomain categories (algebra/ring theory, topology/order, analysis/calculus, number theory/combinatorics, logic/foundations). Our taxonomy contribution is twofold and builds on APRIL's existing categorization rather than constructing error categories from scratch: (i) a domain-stratified cross-tabulation of APRIL's existing error_type categories (lme/mlme/thme/tme) by mathematical subdomain, testing whether mutation category distributions vary significantly across domains (e.g., whether topology has disproportionately more tactic mutation errors while algebra has more line mutation errors); (ii) a finer-grained error taxonomy extracted from the raw 'error' field by parsing Lean compiler messages into semantic categories — typeclass resolution failures, coercion mismatches, tactic incompatibilities, unknown identifier errors, type unification failures, etc. — also stratified by subdomain. The novelty is in the domain stratification and statistical analysis (JSD, predictive power), not in inventing error categories de novo. Our pre-compilation compiler error taxonomy is complementary to Kim et al.'s (2026; arXiv 2604.19459) post-compilation semantic faithfulness taxonomy (mistranslation, fabrication, omission, contradiction): they characterize errors that evade the type-checker (semantic unfaithfulness despite compilation), while we characterize errors caught by the type-checker (compiler failures), stratified by mathematical subdomain. Together, these two taxonomies address different layers of the formalization error stack — and a natural extension is to test whether Kim et al.'s post-compilation error types also exhibit domain-dependent distributions. We cross-reference with FineLeanCorpus's 286k verified entries (which provide hierarchical problem-level domain labels) and Herald's 580k NL-formal pairs (where module paths are recovered by parsing qualified theorem names from formal statements, e.g., extracting 'Topology.Basic' from 'Topology.Basic.isOpen_compl' — an engineering step requiring ~1 additional week beyond direct field access) to measure correlation and divergence between mathematical topic labels, formalization-level module paths, and error patterns. This goes beyond Shebzukhov (2026; arXiv 2603.24372), who reports domain-stratified aggregate cycle consistency scores (number theory 0.722 vs. calculus 0.516) but performs only observational analysis without classifying error categories per domain. **Quantitative success criteria for the error taxonomy** (testable hypotheses that define what constitutes a meaningful finding): (a) **Inter-domain error distribution divergence** — we hypothesize that Jensen-Shannon divergence between error-type distributions across domain pairs will exceed 0.3 (on a [0,1] scale) for at least 3 of 10 domain pairs (e.g., topology vs. algebra, analysis vs. logic), vs. JSD < 0.1 under random domain assignment permutation tests (1000 permutations). Rationale: topology formalizations disproportionately encounter typeclass instance resolution failures (Lean's typeclass system is heavily used for topological spaces, filters, and uniform structures) while algebra formalizations disproportionately encounter coercion chain incompleteness — if these patterns hold, the distributions will diverge substantially. CAM-Bench's finding that applied mathematics domains exhibit qualitatively different error profiles (72.6% library/API grounding failures in optimization/numerical analysis) provides independent support for the hypothesis that error types are domain-dependent. (b) **Predictive power** — we hypothesize that a simple classifier trained on domain → error-type distributions will achieve ≥70% accuracy in predicting the dominant error type for held-out formalizations from a given domain, vs. ~20% baseline (assuming ~5 major error categories). This would demonstrate that knowing a problem's mathematical subdomain provides actionable information about likely failure modes — a qualitative step beyond the aggregate performance differences shown in Shebzukhov (2026). (c) **Actionable recommendations per domain** — for each of the 5 subdomain clusters, we produce a ranked list of the top-5 most frequent error types with concrete mitigation strategies (e.g., 'topology formalizations: prioritize typeclass instance search depth; algebra formalizations: check coercion chain completeness'), evaluated by whether prompting with these recommendations improves formalization accuracy by ≥5 percentage points on held-out examples from that domain vs. prompting without domain-specific error context. If hypotheses (a) and (b) hold, the taxonomy provides the first empirical evidence that autoformalization error types are systematically structured by mathematical subdomain — a finding valuable independent of any downstream pipeline delta, offering actionable guidance for all future domain-specific approaches. The FormalRx challenge (ICML 2026 AI4Math Workshop Track 1) provides a complementary 28-category SCI Error Taxonomy that classifies errors by type alone; our taxonomy is orthogonal in that it stratifies errors by mathematical subdomain, and the two taxonomies can be cross-referenced to test whether certain SCI error categories correlate with specific subdomains. ShadowBench (Track 4 of the same workshop) evaluates end-to-end autoformalization across 8 mathematical areas but does not classify error types. If the hypotheses do not hold (JSD < 0.15 across all domain pairs, prediction accuracy < 40%), we report this as a meaningful negative result: autoformalization errors are domain-invariant, and domain-adaptive approaches should focus on retrieval rather than error-aware prompting. **Stage 2 — Domain-Conditioned Retrieval**: We extend CRAMF's dual-channel hybrid retrieval with a domain-aware reranking layer that boosts same-subdomain definitions. This operates at a fundamentally different level than existing retrieval innovations: CRAMF disambiguates polysemous concepts (concept-level); DRIFT decomposes statements into atomic sub-queries (concept-level decomposition); LeanSearch v2 achieves SOTA domain-agnostic retrieval (retrieval quality); LeanPremise/LeanHammer achieves strong domain-general premise selection for proving (not autoformalization); IndiMathBench provides static category context (static domain awareness). Our reranker adds an orthogonal signal: given that the input problem is dynamically classified as topology, boost ALL topology-related definitions in retrieval, not just disambiguate individual concepts, decompose the statement, or apply a static category context block. **Three specific scenarios motivate dynamic per-problem conditioning over IndiMathBench-style static category context**: (i) **Cross-domain problems** — many formalization targets inherently span multiple mathematical subdomains (e.g., analytic number theory requires both number theory definitions and analysis-level typeclasses; the change of variables formula spans linear algebra, analysis, measure theory, and descriptive set theory; Fermat's Last Theorem formalization requires algebraic number theory crossing algebra, number theory, and analysis). In Mathlib, heavy cross-imports between NumberTheory↔Analysis, Topology↔Algebra, and MeasureTheory↔Topology modules are pervasive. Static category context assigns ONE category and provides fixed definitions, missing cross-domain dependencies. Dynamic conditioning can detect that a specific number theory problem requires analysis-level typeclasses and boost definitions from BOTH domains via soft domain weighting rather than hard category assignment. (ii) **Within-category heterogeneity** — IndiMathBench uses 4 broad categories, but problems within a single category have vastly different definition requirements. Within 'number theory,' elementary number theory (modular arithmetic, Nat.Prime) and analytic number theory (prime number theorem, MeasureTheory.Integral) require completely different Mathlib definitions. Static context provides the same context block regardless; dynamic conditioning at our 5-cluster granularity adapts retrieval per-problem based on the specific subdomain inferred from the problem statement. (iii) **Retrieval precision at higher K** — CRAMF reports only HitRate@3, but complex formalization targets often require 10–20 relevant Mathlib definitions. At K=3, noise is minimal; at K=10 or K=20, the proportion of irrelevant definitions from unrelated domains increases substantially. Domain-conditioned reranking acts as a precision-preserving filter: by downranking definitions from unrelated domains, it maintains higher precision at larger K values, which matters because formalization models are sensitive to irrelevant context in the prompt — adding noisy definitions can hurt performance. We evaluate this directly via HitRate@K and Precision@K curves at K ∈ {3, 5, 10, 20} comparing domain-conditioned vs. domain-agnostic retrieval. The domain classifier for retrieval conditioning uses APRIL's explicit path field as primary training signal, supplemented by Herald's parsed module paths and FineLeanCorpus topic labels. The reranker is trained on this combined data with domain match as an additional feature alongside the existing semantic similarity score. We compare domain-conditioned retrieval vs. domain-agnostic retrieval at matched retrieval budget (same Top-K, same compute) to isolate the domain signal's contribution. We additionally compare against LeanSearch v2's standard mode as a strong domain-agnostic retrieval baseline. **Stage 3 — Domain-Aware Autoformalization**: Using Goedel-Formalizer-V2-8B (with StepFun-Formalizer-7B as additional backbone comparison), we apply domain-prefixed prompting: the input is augmented with predicted subdomain label, top domain-specific error patterns from Stage 1, and domain-conditioned retrieved definitions from Stage 2. We perform LoRA fine-tuning (rank 32) on domain-enriched data combining Herald and FineLeanCorpus, where each training example includes its domain context. No complex LoRA routing or domain-specific adapters — a single adapter learns to use domain context from the prompt. **Evaluation**: We introduce the first systematic multi-domain rotation evaluation protocol for autoformalization — leave-one-domain-out across our 5 subdomain categories, extending ConNF's single-domain OOD paradigm to systematic cross-domain generalization testing. Evaluated on FormalMATH-categorized problems and MathAtlas's 87-area benchmark. MSC-180's 60-branch classification serves as cross-domain generalization test. ConNF serves as an additional single-domain OOD test (New Foundations set theory). We position our evaluation protocol relative to ShadowBench (Track 4): while ShadowBench evaluates across 8 mathematical areas with fixed splits, our leave-one-domain-out rotation provides systematic cross-domain generalization measurement that fixed-split evaluation cannot. Surgical ablations isolate: (a) domain-conditioned retrieval alone (Stage 2 only), (b) domain-prefixed prompting alone (subdomain label in prompt, no retrieval change), (c) domain error context alone (error patterns in prompt, no retrieval change), (d) full combination (Stages 1+2+3), (e) **IndiMathBench-style naive domain prompting baseline** — prepending static category-specific Mathlib context to the input, replicating IndiMathBench's category-based retrieval approach at inference time; this tests whether the simple static approach that dramatically improves compilation also closes the semantic correctness gap, and (f) **LeanSearch v2 retrieval baseline** — replacing our domain-conditioned retrieval with LeanSearch v2's standard mode to test whether superior domain-agnostic retrieval subsumes domain conditioning. If ablation (e) captures 80%+ of semantic correctness gains, we report this honestly as evidence that the simple approach extends to semantic correctness — a valuable finding in itself; if the full pipeline significantly outperforms, it validates the engineering investment in dynamic conditioning and error taxonomy. We specifically test whether the three scenarios motivating dynamic conditioning (cross-domain problems, within-category heterogeneity, high-K precision) explain the performance delta: by stratifying results into single-domain vs. cross-domain problems (classified by whether their Mathlib dependencies span multiple subdomain clusters), we can directly measure whether dynamic conditioning's advantage concentrates on cross-domain cases as hypothesized. A domain-agnostic matched-compute baseline (same LoRA budget, same retrieval budget, no domain conditioning) serves as control. Per-domain improvement analysis focuses on whether currently weak domains (analysis, discrete math, topology, geometry) show disproportionate gains. Domain-conditioned retrieval HitRate@K and Precision@K metrics at K ∈ {3, 5, 10, 20} provide pipeline-internal evaluation independent of downstream formalization accuracy.",

We introduce the first systematic multi-domain rotation evaluation protocol (leave-one-domain-out across ≥5 categories), more rigorous than ShadowBench's (Track 4) fixed-split 8-area evaluation. Six surgical ablations include an IndiMathBench-style static domain context baseline and LeanSearch v2 retrieval replacement, with results stratified by single-domain vs. cross-domain problems to directly test whether dynamic conditioning's advantage concentrates on cross-domain cases.
